query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of coherent nanoprecipitations, such as δ-lamellae and γ″ particles, can overcome the limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, while retaining or increasing strength.

generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces of the nanoprecipitations facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations, while the nanoprecipitations themselves provide order hardening and lattice misfit strengthening, leading to improved strength and ductility. Question: Can independently controllable multiple coherent precipitation structures be tailored by stepwise thermo-mechanical processes to generate ultrahigh strength and ductile refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (at.%) refractory high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase bcc/fcc structure. Processing: Arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 5 h, hot rolling at 1200 °C (80% reduction), cold rolling at 25 °C (75% reduction), annealing at 900 °C for 5 min, and aging at 650 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); microstructural characterization via EBSD, TEM, STEM, and APT. Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
